name: Robot Dispatch
trigger: The deployment window opens for the market. The shift has three phases: deployment in the morning, field operations all day, undeployment at night.
purpose: Robot pays for Usable Supply Hours, the time robots are parked at a merchant and able to take orders. A robot at 15% battery, holding food, stuck, or parked at the wrong merchant earns zero USH. Dispatch is the loop that keeps the fleet healthy and parked where it can take orders. A bad dispatcher does not just miss tasks, they burn USH by deploying to the wrong restaurant or pulling a robot off an active delivery. Scope: Robot, all markets, Build dispatch team.
doneWhen: Undeployment is complete for the market, the field task queue is at zero or every open task has a documented reason, and the handoff is posted in Slack.
timeToRun: One shift. No fixed window for Robot; shift length and handoff time are TBD.

steps.title: Read the shift instructions
steps.trigger: Shift start, first thing.
steps.work: Open the dispatch Slack channel and read the market's standing instructions for the day. Note anything that changes the default priorities, and confirm whether the market is deploy/undeploy or leave-out. Prep the first wave before operators clock in; 15 to 20 minutes early is normal. In Chicago, wait for the operator to confirm battery rotation and van loading are done before sending the wave.
steps.doneWhen: You can say what this market needs today beyond the default battery and task work.

steps.title: Which kind of market is this?
steps.trigger: The standing instructions have been read.
steps.work: The city sets this, not Robot or Build, and it does not change without a permit change. A deploy/undeploy market requires every robot indoors overnight, so robots deploy out of the MRO each morning: Chicago and Hoboken. A leave-out market has robots living on the street overnight at rally points or overnight merchants, with no morning deployment: Miami, Jersey City, Washington DC and San Jose. The distinction changes almost every step that follows.
rules: Know which kind of market you are running before you touch anything.

steps.title: Morning health scan of the fleet
steps.trigger: A leave-out market, where robots are already on the street.
steps.work: Scan the fleet's health in Mission Control. There is no deployment phase here; the robots are already out. After rain, check any robot an operator touches for a swap or task rather than running a dedicated water ingress sweep.

steps.title: Can this robot take a trip?
steps.trigger: Before every deploy or undeploy trip.
steps.work: Check the robot's health in MRO before any trip. Check all three: health shows healthy in MRO, battery is 20% or above, and it is not grounded. Unhealthy robots block the trip, and Mission Control rejects it automatically. Stella proposes, the dispatcher approves.

steps.title: Reboot from MRO and re-check
steps.trigger: A robot failed the health check.
steps.work: Try a reboot from MRO, then re-run the health check. What symptoms mean a field visit rather than a pickup is TBD for the owner to fill in.

steps.title: Ask the dispatch lead about the health readout
steps.trigger: You cannot tell whether the robot is fit for a trip.
steps.work: Post the robot ID and the MRO health readout in the dispatch channel and ask the dispatch lead.

steps.title: Deploy robots from the MRO to merchants
steps.trigger: The robot passed its health check and the deployment window is open.
steps.work: Deploy healthy robots out to their assigned merchants. The procedure, batch size and order of merchants are TBD for the owner to fill in. Deploying too many from one MRO at once has caused problems; the cap is TBD.
rules: Never deploy more than the market cap of robots from one MRO at once.
steps.doneWhen: Every robot shows parked at its assigned merchant in Mission Control.

steps.title: Pull the low-battery list
steps.trigger: Start of field operations, and again each time the action list runs down.
steps.work: In Mission Control, apply the low-battery filter, a fixed cutoff around 35%. Then scan the rest manually and pull the lowest 10 robots above the cutoff. Sort lowest to highest. Low battery does not generate a task on its own: if you do not build this list, nobody swaps the battery. Do not wait for robots to go low. The fleet depletes at roughly the same rate, so if one is low they all are, and you spend the night chasing unhealthy robots while USH bleeds across the fleet. Swapping ahead also evens out charging and means fewer swaps at undeployment.
rules: Never assume a robot below 20% can make a trip; it is unhealthy and needs a swap, not a deploy.
steps.doneWhen: A sorted list of every robot under 35% plus the 10 lowest above it, with robot ID, battery and current merchant.

steps.title: Does this robot go on the action list now?
steps.trigger: The low-battery list and the pending task queue are in hand.
steps.work: Pick 5 to 10 robots to action now. Check all: battery is under 35% or a pending task is attached; it is not on an active delivery, meaning the task status is not Scheduled with an empty bot; it is not grounded with a type needing engineer review; and the list is 10 or fewer. Tracking every dispatched robot in real time is too manual, so work in batches, finish the batch, then rebuild. A wave is about 10 items per operator and both operators get their own wave.

next.label: Any no: leave it for the next pass

steps.title: Ask the dispatch lead about the robot
steps.trigger: You cannot tell whether a robot belongs on the action list.
steps.work: Post the robot ID, battery, task status and merchant in the dispatch channel and ask the dispatch lead.

steps.title: Dispatch a field operator
steps.trigger: The action list is approved.
steps.work: For each robot on the list, create a task in Portal with robot ID, location, task type and battery, then post the assignment in the dispatch Slack channel. Field operators are NO assets and work from the Portal task. If an operator is already at a robot for a task, swap the battery too even if it is above the threshold. Never send anyone back to the same robot twice. Locations go to operators as a Google Maps pin, not MRO coordinates.
steps.when: Immediately after the action list is approved
rules: Never dispatch against a robot whose task is Scheduled with an empty bot; that is an active delivery and interrupting it kills the order and the USH.

steps.title: Is the robot where the task says?
steps.trigger: The field operator reports on arrival.
steps.work: When the operator reports the robot is not where the task says, check its return trip distance in Mission Control. Under about 0.1 miles the operator waits for it; further than that, re-queue the robot and move the operator to the next task. The 0.1 miles is a feel rather than a measured threshold and is TBD to confirm.

next.label: Yes, or a short wait under 0.1 mi

steps.title: Re-queue the robot and move the operator on
steps.trigger: The robot moved too far for the operator to wait.
steps.work: Put the robot back on the list for the next pass and send the operator to the next task.

steps.title: Triage the task queue by type
steps.trigger: A pending task is attached to a robot on the list.
steps.work: Work pending tasks in Mission Control by type. Pending is the only state you action. For food removal, a pending robot that has stopped moving gets actioned; pending but still moving means wait, because it will not be where you send the operator. A robot stops in place when the failure was robot-side, and returns to its origin merchant when the failure was customer-side such as a no-show or lid problem.
rules: Never touch a robot whose empty-bot task is Scheduled.

next.label: Swap, flag, unflip or clean camera
Return to parking lot, or unstuck
Scheduled with empty bot: leave it alone

steps.title: Can it be piloted instead of visited?
steps.trigger: A return-to-parking-lot or unstuck task is pending.
steps.work: Check the location and camera feed in DriveU first. An unobstructed path means a pilot clears the task without spending an operator. A third case exists for return to parking lot: the robot never left the merchant, so no return is needed at all. The dispatch lead makes this call. For clean camera, check the feed first and only send an operator if it is actually dirty.

next.label: Path clear: pilot it and clear the task
Obstructed: send an operator with a van
Never left the merchant: no return needed

steps.title: Collect the robot onto the pickup list
steps.trigger: A robot grounded mid-trip and needs a van.
steps.work: Not every operator has a van. Collect grounded robots through the shift and send the full list to the dispatch lead at end of shift. Pickups run as one sweep on the next van shift.

steps.title: Action the emergency RECO first
steps.trigger: A RECO is posted in the dispatch Slack channel.
steps.work: Drop the current batch and action the RECO first. RECOs arrive only through Slack and are invisible in MRO and Mission Control, so watching only the tools will miss them. The dispatcher is not in Slack, so the dispatch lead relays. Most emergencies also generate a normal task, unstuck, unflip or empty bot, so it gets done within about an hour regardless, but the dispatcher cannot tell it is an emergency from the task alone. If it needs to jump the queue, say so.
rules: RECOs are top priority and never appear in MRO or Mission Control.

steps.title: Can this robot be ungrounded now?
steps.trigger: A repair ticket has closed on a grounded robot.
steps.work: Check all: the grounding type is not modem failure or another type flagged for engineer review; the robot is not on a trip; and the repair ticket in the Work Order Tool is resolved. Ungrounding means changing state twice in MRO, grounded to ready to deploy to parked. Ready to deploy means at an MRO or in a van and not accepting orders; parked means in the field and accepting orders. Stella proposes, the dispatcher approves.
rules: Never change a robot's state while it is on a trip.
Never act on a modem-failure grounding without fleet quality engineer sign-off.

steps.title: Change state to ready to deploy, then parked
steps.trigger: The robot cleared the ungrounding checks.
steps.work: In MRO, change state twice: grounded to ready to deploy, then to parked. What actually happens on a mid-trip state change is unknown; nobody has tested it on purpose and nobody should.
steps.doneWhen: The robot shows parked in MRO and accepts orders in Mission Control.

steps.title: Leave it grounded and route to the engineer
steps.trigger: The grounding type needs review, or the ticket is still open.
steps.work: Leave the robot grounded. Modem failures go to Robot's fleet quality engineer through the ticket system before anyone acts. Both this and the no-state-change-mid-trip rule exist because of the train incident.

steps.title: Ask the dispatch lead about the grounding
steps.trigger: You do not recognise the grounding type.
steps.work: Leave it grounded and post the robot ID, grounding reason and ticket link in the dispatch channel.

steps.title: Redeploy a robot to a different merchant
steps.trigger: A robot is parked at the wrong merchant.
steps.work: Deploy the robot to its target merchant via Mission Control. A robot attached to merchant A cannot be redeployed to merchant A; the tool rejects it. Park it at a different merchant first, then send it with a pilot to the intended one. That workaround is the process.
steps.doneWhen: The robot shows parked at the correct merchant in Mission Control.

steps.title: Is it undeploy time yet?
steps.trigger: A batch of field work is finished.
steps.work: Rebuild the action list when a wave runs down, not before. When the market's undeploy time arrives, move to Phase 3. The exact time is TBD per market.

steps.title: Undeploy the fleet for the night
steps.trigger: The market's undeploy time.
steps.work: Map each robot to its overnight destination and deploy via the Mission Control deploy function, one destination at a time. Run the health check on each robot first. Anything outside the market's zones gets a pickup task instead. In a deploy/undeploy market every robot must be inside the MRO by the city's deadline, routed to rally points then vanned in or tripped straight to the MRO; a robot left outside overnight is a compliance problem, not just lost USH. In a leave-out market the destination is the rally point or overnight merchant. Current practice is one rally point at a time, and why is TBD.
steps.doneWhen: Every robot has a destination and a trip started, or a pickup task in Portal.

steps.title: Monitor return trips
steps.trigger: The first undeploy trip is under way.
steps.work: Watch trip status in Mission Control, refreshing manually because it never auto-refreshes. Flag any robot that stalls, stops short or misses its destination. A clean night with zero pickups is rare; expect a few.

steps.title: Did every robot arrive?
steps.trigger: Return trips are being watched.
steps.work: Every robot either shows arrived or goes on the flagged list for troubleshooting.

steps.title: Work the flagged robot
steps.trigger: A robot missed its rally point or stalled mid-trip.
steps.work: Check health in MRO, reboot if unhealthy, pilot if possible, otherwise raise a pickup task. In Miami, a robot that stopped mid-trip showing healthy with no task generated is probably a failed bridge crossing between Brickell and downtown: Robot cancels the trip manually and no return-to-parking-lot task fires, so it is only caught by eye. Treat it as a return to parking lot and decide fast, because the robot is still trip-eligible.

steps.title: Post the overnight handoff
steps.trigger: Every robot has arrived or is flagged with a reason.
steps.work: Post the overnight list in the dispatch Slack channel: every robot, its confirmed location, and any open pickups or unresolved groundings. The morning crew uses this to locate, clean and prep.
rules: Every location on the list is one you clicked into and confirmed, never one read off the merchant assignment.
